title: Catching the repricing wave: insights from daily online supermarket prices
gist: ECB staff using daily online supermarket prices find the food repricing wave after the 2026 Middle East energy shock is weaker than after Russia's 2022 invasion: price-increase frequency rose in March 2026 then stabilised, without the broadening seen in 2022. Little evidence so far of persistent repricing changes.

insights.claim: Daily supermarket price data show the food repricing triggered by the 2026 energy shock from the war in the Middle East is weaker than the wave after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Suggests less food-driven inflation persistence than 2022, reducing hawkish pressure from this channel.
insights.quote: So far, the rise in the repricing momentum has been weaker than in 2022

insights.claim: Food repricing initially rose fairly broadly in March 2026 but then stabilised, whereas in 2022 the repricing wave kept rising.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Stabilisation points to a contained rather than escalating pass-through.

insights.claim: The frequency of food price increases rose in March 2026 shortly after the energy shock, but by much less than in the 2022 surge; the gap between frequency of increases and decreases is small.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Net upward repricing pressure looks modest.

insights.claim: The average size of food price increases changed relatively little in 2026, similar to 2022, so the difference between episodes lies in the frequency (extensive margin) of repricing, not the size.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Inflation differences stem from how many items reprice, not magnitude per change.

insights.claim: In 2026 the frequency of price increases did not rise and widen sequentially across food categories as it did in 2022; the cross-category range is more compressed and maximum frequencies are far lower in most months.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: No sign of a spreading, broad-based repricing wave through September 2026.

insights.claim: The ECB finds little evidence so far of a persistent change in how often retailers reprice food items after the 2026 energy shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Supports a view that second-round food inflation risk is limited for now; 'so far' hedges the call.
insights.quote: we find little evidence so far of a persistent change in how often retailers reprice food items

insights.claim: Large cost shocks lead firms to reprice earlier than planned (state-dependent pricing), raising the frequency of price increases and producing non-linear inflation responses relevant for monetary policy; small shocks leave regular repricing plans unchanged.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Shock size thresholds determine whether pass-through accelerates.
insights.locator: How do firms react to a cost shock?

insights.claim: In 2022, categories with at least 10% of products raising prices expanded and stayed large for several months, a broad and persistent shift consistent with state-dependent pricing during the 2021-24 inflation cycle.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The 2022 pattern is the benchmark of a persistent repricing regime; 2026 lacks it.

insights.claim: Firms' decisions depend on shock size, competitors' prices and menu costs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Frames the drivers of pass-through speed.
insights.locator: How do firms react to a cost shock?

themes.theme: Why the margin of inflation matters for policy

insights.claim: Inflation can rise through more frequent repricing, larger individual price changes, broad-based increases or surges in specific products, so policymakers need to identify which margin drives it, not just that inflation rose.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Margin decomposition helps judge persistence and the policy response.

insights.claim: The contrast between 2022 and 2026 is consistent with the finding that the effects of an energy shock depend on the shock's composition and the economic conditions prevailing when it occurs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Initial conditions matter, so 2022 analogies may overstate current pass-through.

insights.claim: Food accounts for around 20% of expenditure in the euro area HICP basket, a larger share for low-income households, and food prices strongly shape households' inflation perceptions and expectations.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Food price moves can feed inflation expectations disproportionately.

insights.claim: After an energy shock food prices are among the first to rise.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Food is an early indicator of energy pass-through.

insights.claim: The ECB's Daily Price Dataset, built with the BIS Innovation Hub and Deutsche Bundesbank under Project Spectrum, uses daily online supermarket prices and an AI classifier mapping product descriptions to HICP consumption categories.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Central banks are using AI-enabled high-frequency micro data for real-time inflation nowcasting.
insights.locator: How do firms react to a cost shock?

insights.claim: The DPD measures repricing frequencies monthly, excluding temporary sales, but can update the current month's estimate continuously because observations are collected daily.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Gives a timely read ahead of official HICP releases.
insights.locator: How do firms react to a cost shock?
